analysis.one_liner: Lets antitrust regulators police nonprofit hospital mergers and anticompetitive behavior.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let the FTC police competition among tax-exempt hospital groups, sat in the House Judiciary Committee and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Federal Trade Commission Act so that tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations count as companies the FTC can enforce competition law against. Right now, nonprofits in this space can largely escape FTC antitrust review, which lets hospital mergers and pricing practices go unchallenged. The bill never received any committee action after its referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employers, and insurers paying hospital bills would benefit if FTC enforcement slows hospital mergers and anticompetitive contracting that tend to raise prices. Hospital workers in consolidated markets could also gain from reduced monopsony pressure on wages.

how_it_helps.text: Closes a legal exemption that currently lets tax-exempt hospital organizations escape Federal Trade Commission enforcement against anticompetitive practices.
By subjecting nonprofit hospital systems to competition law, it targets the hospital consolidation that tends to raise the prices patients and insurers pay.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt nonprofit hospital systems, which would face FTC competition enforcement for the first time, potentially limiting their ability to merge or negotiate as consolidated systems.

drawbacks.text: Applying antitrust rules to nonprofit hospitals could complicate mergers that keep small rural facilities financially viable, an objection hospital groups typically raise.
The bill was extremely narrow, addressing one loophole, and drew almost no cosponsors, suggesting it would have limited reach even if enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—restoring FTC antitrust oversight of nonprofit hospitals—would likely be modest in scope but real, targeting a sector where consolidation has raised prices. The cost is that hospitals could face legal uncertainty in legitimate mergers. On balance, the public interest in lower healthcare prices outweighs that cost, but the bill was never seriously pursued.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 26, 2023, and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
The only action ever taken was that referral; no hearing, markup, vote, or committee report followed.
It expired with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonprofit hospital systems keep their current exemption from FTC antitrust enforcement, and consolidation in hospital markets can continue unchecked.

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bring nonprofit hospitals under FTC antitrust authority.

for.name: 1 of 224 House Republicans and 1 additional House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to three members.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no further action—no hearing, markup, or vote—letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had both a Democratic sponsor and a Republican cosponsor, but with only three total cosponsors it never got far enough for a party-line fight to emerge.

industries.note: The bill would strip nonprofit hospitals of their current exemption from FTC antitrust enforcement, exposing their mergers and contracting practices to competition law. Patients and insurers would benefit if it reduced hospital consolidation-driven price increases.
For-profit hospitals are already subject to FTC antitrust review, so the bill would level the playing field slightly rather than change their position directly.
